scope: One additional Indo-West Pacific fish for the guide, illustrative reef encounters and optional identification/recall. Illustrate a blue-and-yellow ribbon eel partly exposed from a fixed burrow. Do not assign sex from colour or show the exposed model as the complete one-metre animal.
iucnYearConvention: Use LC with assessment year 2009, assessed 2009-02-04, original publication 2010 and an errata version published in 2017. The assessment date comes from the current FishBase IUCN 2025-2 export; Museums Victoria independently reports LC. Direct IUCN page, DOI and PDF access failed during this review, so do not describe the entire primary assessment as personally read or treat the 2017 errata as a new assessment.

specimens.name: Ribbon eel
marks: Two tubular nostrils widen into conspicuous fan-shaped flaps
The exposed body is extremely slender and flattened from side to side
A ribbon-like back fin begins near the head and follows the body
Small fleshy projections extend from the snout tip and the front of the lower jaw
specimens.role: Small-fish predator associated with reef burrows.
specimens.fact: Colour alone is an unreliable sex label: a captive breeding study found that body colour did not consistently match sex or sexual maturity.
specimens.habitat: Tropical Indo-West Pacific lagoon and seaward reefs, using burrows in sand or rubble beside coral reefs.
specimens.diet: Small fishes. It is a predator rather than a plankton-feeding garden eel.
specimens.behavior: Usually shelters with its head or part of its slender body protruding from a burrow. This resting view shows an exposed forebody; much of the animal remains concealed.
specimens.observe: Find the flared nostrils and little jaw projections first, then compare its narrow ribbon-shaped body with the giant moray’s heavier head and mottled body. Black, blue-and-yellow and largely yellow appearances are reported, so combine shape and colour rather than relying on one hue.

claimSupport.acceptedName: Eschmeyer's current catalog accepts Rhinomuraena quaesita Garman, 1888; Smith's primary 2012 global checklist agrees and treats Rhinomuraena ambonensis as its synonym.
claimSupport.marks: Shen and colleagues' primary redescription documents the very slender eel, expanded anterior nasal flaps, a snout-tip projection and three lower-jaw appendages. Current museum accounts and identified photographs corroborate the conspicuous nostrils and colour phases. The fin and fine mouth anatomy remain simplified learning characters, not a complete taxonomic key.
claimSupport.roleDiet: The Australian Museum identifies a predator. FishBase's species account explicitly reports small fishes, citing Chen and colleagues' primary Taiwan revision and reef-fish literature. The garden-eel contrast is a feeding-strategy distinction, not a proposed close relationship.
claimSupport.habitatBehavior: Australian Museum and Museums Victoria describe sandy or rubble burrows beside reefs. FishBase supports lagoon/seaward reefs and partial emergence. The fixed illustrated burrow does not assert that the eel never leaves its shelter.
claimSupport.colourSex: Shen et al. (1979) interpreted aquarium colour changes and gonadal histology as protandry. Sadovy de Mitcheson and Liu's 2008 review considered protandry unconfirmed; FishBase carries that qualification. Preininger et al. (2015) directly report that captive colour variation did not reflect sex or maturity. Museum summaries still associate phases with sexes. Public copy therefore reports appearances and the later study's limit, without assigning the model sex, a universal transition sequence or a size threshold for changing sex.
claimSupport.sizeDepth: Museums Victoria gives 130 cm total length and 1–57 m; Australian Museum independently gives 1.3 m. Current FishBase gives 1–67 m, so 57 m is the selected museum metadata interval, not a biological hard limit. Nominal one-metre total length and approximately 0.45 m exposed forebody are illustrative choices within this scale, not specimen measurements or equal suitability throughout the depth interval.
claimSupport.iucn: LC is independently reported by Museums Victoria and FishBase. FishBase's current indexed IUCN 2025-2 export specifies 4 February 2009. The published citation is McCosker (2010), errata 2017; those dates are kept separate.
claimSupport.comparison: A one-way giant_moray link contrasts an extremely narrow ribbon eel with the existing larger-headed moray record. Preserve that older record exactly. This comparison does not claim that the two are each other's nearest species-level lookalike.

specimens.caution: No sex, maturity or reproductive-state diagnosis from the blue/yellow palette. No universal black-to-blue-to-yellow timeline, lifespan, lifelong burrow occupancy, aggression, venom, aquarium-care or enhanced-colour-vision claim. The hidden posterior body is deliberately omitted rather than shrunk into the exposed section. Keep nasal fans distinct from eyes and jaw appendages; do not add snake tongues, horns or ordinary fish pectoral/pelvic fins.

modelProvenance.nominalDimension: Approximate COMPLETE total body length including the concealed posterior body, not the visible model height or the burrow-base footprint
modelProvenance.representative: One unsexed blue-bodied appearance with a yellow back fin, snout and lower jaw. No gonadal anatomy, eggs or phase-to-sex key. Other documented appearances remain described in the guide.
modelProvenance.basis: A one-metre total-length individual is illustrative within the published 1.3 m size scale. About 0.4–0.5 m of curving forebody is exposed; the remaining length is concealed. Use a fixed subdued burrow lip at substrate level, and fit the viewer to actual visible geometry. The selected museum depth range is not a claim that this pose occurs uniformly from 1 to 57 m.
modelProvenance.anatomy: Laterally compressed, very thin continuous forebody rising in a relaxed curve; a slender tapered head with separate jaws and recessed mouth; small lateral eyes; paired tubular anterior nostrils with outward flared fan margins; a single slender snout-tip projection and three distinct lower-jaw projections at the front join, with lateral projections angled forward/downward; back fin beginning anterior to the small gill opening and continuing along the exposed body. Omit the hidden tail rather than inventing a visible complete tail. No pectoral or pelvic fins.
modelProvenance.anatomyLimits: Small teeth, pores and fin rays can be simplified. Keep nasal fans separate from the mouth and eyes. Forebody dimensions and curvature are illustrative, not a diagnostic measurement. No oversized dragon head, horns, snake tongue, facial whisker forest, external ears or ordinary tail paddle.
modelProvenance.motion: Keep the substrate/burrow root fixed. Use subtle localized head/jaw or nasal movement and restrained upper-body sway if supported without vertex uploads. Reduced-motion and inspection poses remain static; no whole-body burrow relocation or new swimming simulation is required.

integration.maintainedSource: Append the specimen and used references without regenerating old guide records.
integration.practice: Inspection and recall remain optional and do not award discoveries or persist current card state, reflections or ordering.
integration.lookalikeNote: One-way giant_moray teaching contrast; preserve that prior record exactly.
integration.identificationLimit: Combine structural features, multiple appearances and locality with specialist resources. This model does not establish wild identity, sex or maturity by itself.
